questions.question:
**In the following ****question, some part of the sentence may have errors. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and select the appropriate option. If a sentence is free from error, select 'No Error'.**

What a comfort to see that you (1)/ have organizing and planning (2)/ everything for us. (3)/ No Error (4)
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Option 2, i.e., **‘have organizing and planning’.**

Part 2 of the sentence has an error because it confuses the tense of the verbs- the present perfect continuous, the present perfect, or the present continuous? The sentence can only have one of these tenses.

Moreover, continuous forms of a verb, such as ‘organizing’ or ‘planning’, are never used with only ‘have’, as they have been used here.

Possible ways to correct the sentence are : **‘What a comfort to see that you have organised everything for us’.**

**In the following question, some part of the sentence may have errors. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and select the appropriate option. If a sentence is free from error, select 'No Error'.**

Please note that you will be eligible for (1)/ the voucher only if you (2)/ had received this email. (3)/ No Error (4)
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Option 3, i.e., **‘had received this email’.**

Part 1 is in the simple future tense. Moreover, the sentence is a conditional sentence.

In a conditional sentence, the simple future is only succeeded by the present simple. 

Therefore, Part 3 has an error because it uses the past perfect tense instead of present simple: ‘had received’ and not ‘receive’.

The correct sentence would be **‘Please note that you will be eligible for the voucher only if you receive this email.’**

questions.solution:

Part 3 uses the wrong possessive pronoun: ‘our’ instead of ‘your’.

In Part 3, **‘in our account’ **should be replaced by **‘in your account’**.

The use of the pronoun ‘you’ in Part 2 tells us that the sentence is addressed to someone.

We can infer from Part 1 that the sentence is spoken by someone who works in some security personnel or organization.

It is intended to assure the addressee that the organization takes security seriously, which is why they want to keep that person informed about any activity in his/her (bank, email, etc.) account.

So, the right pronoun will be ‘your’ and not ‘our’, as the statement is addressed to ‘you’ and the account belongs to the same person.

The correct sentence will be **‘We take security very seriously and we want to keep you in the loop on important actions in your account’.**

There are two actions which are described in the sentence: 1) the Pooja getting over and 2) people coming out.

So, the correct sentence would be: **‘After the Pooja in the temple got over, people started coming out to get their slippers’.**

questions.solution:

The correct answer is Option 2, i.e., **‘are’.**

The given sentence needs improvement because it does not follow the agreement of the verb with the subject.

When one of the subjects joined by ‘nor’ is plural, the verb must be plural.

Here, the subject ‘the boys’ is in the plural.

Therefore, the verb must agree to it and the right form of the verb will be plural (**‘are’ **instead of **‘is’**).

So, the correct sentence will be **‘Neither teacher nor the boys are in a mood to play’.**

questions.question:
**The question below consists of a set of labelled sentences. Out of the four options given, select the most logical order of the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.**

**Reading forces us to**

P: or heard in our lives

Q: we might not have seen

R: look at words that
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Option 2, i.e., **RQP.**

The part of the sentence given to us is **‘Reading forces us to’**.

The next set of words must tell us what it is that reading forces us to do, and the words ‘forces us to’ necessitate that the word right after them should be a verb.

Therefore, the next in order is R, or ‘look at words that’, as R begins with a verb (‘look’) and begins telling us what reading forces us to do.

R ends with ‘words that’. The next set of words must describe the ‘words’ reading forces us to look at, and should complete the ‘that-’ clause.

This is done by Q, or ‘we might not have seen’. It completes the ‘that-’ clause with which R ends.

The last in order is therefore P, or ‘or heard in our lives’, which only provides additional information.

The correct order is RQP, and the resultant sentence is **‘Reading forces us to look at words that we might not have seen or heard in our lives’**, which is both coherent and grammatically correct
